learn/market-foundations.html:
TRADE ZUKO / Foundations

How financial markets work

Stocks, indices, derivatives and the mechanics behind a quoted price.

BY AMAN SINGH SUNEOLEARN · OBSERVE · REVIEW
ORIGINAL LEARNING GRAPHIC / NOT MARKET DATA
IN THIS CHAPTER01 · Start with the instrument, not the tip02 · Exchanges, brokers and the order book03 · Trading styles are time horizons, not skill levels04 · Build an information hierarchyPractice & learning check

Original educational notes
Reviewed 21 September 2026

01 / Foundations

Start with the instrument, not the tip

A share represents an ownership interest in a company. A bond is a debt claim. An index is a calculation describing a basket of securities; it is not itself a share you can buy. Funds and derivatives can reference an index, but their structures and risks differ. A derivative obtains its value from an underlying asset or reference, with additional contract terms.

  • Stocks: business performance, valuation, liquidity and corporate-event risk.
  • Futures: a contract with obligations, margin and mark-to-market exposure.
  • Options: rights for buyers and obligations for sellers, with an expiry date.
  • Crypto and currencies: different market structures, custody arrangements and legal requirements.
02 / Foundations

Exchanges, brokers and the order book

An exchange brings together trading interests under its rules. A broker provides access; clearing and settlement determine how obligations are met. A screen price is usually a past transaction or a current quote, not a guaranteed execution price. The bid is a buying quote; the ask is a selling quote. Their gap is the spread.

  • NSE and BSE are Indian exchanges; their product and segment rules differ.
  • NIFTY 50, NIFTY Bank and SENSEX measure different baskets. A move in one does not mean every constituent moved.
  • Demat holdings, a cash trading account and a derivatives position are different records. Learn your broker’s workflow.
WORKED EXAMPLE / FICTIONAL

Suppose the best bid is 99.90 and ask is 100.10. An immediate buy may transact near the ask, not at the last traded price of 100.00. Larger orders can reach worse prices deeper in the book.

03 / Foundations

Trading styles are time horizons, not skill levels

Scalping involves very short holding periods and many execution decisions. Intraday positions are normally opened and closed within the session. Swing and positional approaches hold longer and face overnight gaps and corporate events. Investing typically focuses on a longer-term ownership thesis. More frequent trading means costs and mistakes can accumulate faster.

  • Choose a study horizon before comparing charts. A daily chart and a five-minute chart answer different questions.
  • Market hours, settlement cycles, permitted order types and contract sizes may change; verify them with the exchange and broker.
  • A course, a chart pattern or a profitable example does not establish that trading is suitable for someone.
04 / Foundations

Build an information hierarchy

Use exchange announcements and company filings for corporate facts; use official economic releases for macro data. Separate a verified fact, an interpretation and an untested opinion. Social posts and screenshots can omit losses, costs or timing.

  • Ask: what instrument, what timestamp, which source and which assumptions?
  • Do not send money, account credentials, OTPs or remote access to someone promising guaranteed returns.
  • Understand costs, taxation and complaint channels before opening or using a real account.

PAUSE / APPLY / REFLECT

Make it your own.

Choose a fictional company and an index. Write three ways their risk differs. Then explain why buying a share is different from buying an option on it.

Does a last-traded price guarantee the price of your next order?

learn/candles-and-charts.title: Read candles without guessing
learn/candles-and-charts.html:
TRADE ZUKO / Foundations

Read candles without guessing

OHLC, candle context, chart types, timeframes and common interpretation mistakes.

BY AMAN SINGH SUNEOLEARN · OBSERVE · REVIEW
ORIGINAL LEARNING GRAPHIC / NOT MARKET DATA
IN THIS CHAPTER01 · Four prices, one interval02 · Single- and multi-candle shapes03 · Timeframes change the story04 · Standard versus transformed chartsPractice & learning check

Original educational notes
Reviewed 21 September 2026

01 / Foundations

Four prices, one interval

A standard candlestick describes the open, high, low and close over a chosen time interval. Its body joins open and close; its wick spans the extremes. If close is above open, the interval finished higher. That is a description of the past, not a forecast of the next candle.

  • A long body describes a larger net move relative to nearby candles.
  • A long wick shows an excursion away from the body; it does not identify who traded or prove manipulation.
  • A doji has open and close close together. Its importance depends on location and context.
WORKED EXAMPLE / FICTIONAL

A candle with open 100, high 110, low 96 and close 106 rose by 6 units over the interval. Its range was 14 units. Neither value tells you what tomorrow will do.

02 / Foundations

Single- and multi-candle shapes

Hammer, shooting star and pin-bar names describe body-and-wick geometry. Engulfing patterns compare adjacent real bodies. An inside bar has its high and low within the previous bar’s range. Morning and evening stars use a three-candle sequence. Definitions vary slightly between textbooks and platforms.

  • Shape: describe the actual prices and relative sizes.
  • Location: ask whether it appears after a trend, at a zone or in random congestion.
  • Follow-through: study subsequent action without pretending the outcome was knowable in advance.
  • Failure: keep examples where the expected direction did not occur.
03 / Foundations

Timeframes change the story

A small upward candle can exist inside a large downward daily candle. Higher-timeframe context and a lower-timeframe observation are not contradictions. Match the timeframe to the question. A screenshot with no axis, timestamp or surrounding bars gives limited evidence.

  • Start with a higher-timeframe map, then inspect a lower-timeframe sequence.
  • Compare candles from the same data source and session definition.
  • A still-forming candle can change its shape before it closes.
04 / Foundations

Standard versus transformed charts

Line charts simplify prices, often using closes. OHLC bars and standard candles retain interval extremes. Heikin Ashi and some other chart styles transform prices; their displayed values may not be executable market prices. Logarithmic scales compare proportional moves while linear scales compare absolute changes.

  • Use standard, time-based OHLC when checking simple order-fill assumptions.
  • Do not infer a guaranteed entry price from a smoothed chart.
  • Use the pattern atlas as a vocabulary guide, not a buy/sell checklist.

PAUSE / APPLY / REFLECT

Make it your own.

Draw an up candle and a down candle with the same high and low. Mark open, close, body and wicks. Find a case where an attractive candle is followed by a move in the opposite direction.

learn/price-action.title: Structure, zones and price action
learn/price-action.html:
TRADE ZUKO / Technical analysis

Structure, zones and price action

Higher highs, ranges, breakouts, retests, liquidity language and failed setups.

BY AMAN SINGH SUNEOLEARN · OBSERVE · REVIEW
ORIGINAL LEARNING GRAPHIC / NOT MARKET DATA
IN THIS CHAPTER01 · Map the sequence before naming a pattern02 · Support and resistance are areas03 · Breakout, retest and failure04 · Liquidity concepts without storytellingPractice & learning check

Original educational notes
Reviewed 21 September 2026

01 / Technical analysis

Map the sequence before naming a pattern

An uptrend is often described by rising swing highs and lows; a downtrend by falling swing highs and lows. A range lacks sustained progress in either direction. The swing-identification rule matters: changing the lookback can change your labels. Record that rule before reviewing results.

  • Higher high / higher low: a sequence, not a guarantee of continuation.
  • Lower high / lower low: a sequence, not a reason by itself to short.
  • Break of structure and change of character are descriptive terms with non-universal definitions. Specify exactly which swing and which close you mean.
02 / Technical analysis

Support and resistance are areas

Support describes an area where prior declines met buying interest; resistance describes an area where advances met selling interest. Previous-session extremes, repeated turning points and round numbers can attract attention. None is an impenetrable wall.

  • Use a zone whose width reflects the instrument and timeframe.
  • Prior highs and lows are reference points, not certain pools of executable orders.
  • A broken resistance area may later behave as support, but a retest is not assured.
WORKED EXAMPLE / FICTIONAL

In a fictional range from 100 to 110, a print at 110.20 is not automatically a durable breakout. Price can return below 110 before or after the candle closes.

03 / Technical analysis

Breakout, retest and failure

A breakout means price moved beyond a chosen boundary. A retest means it revisited that area. To study either, define what counts as a break, whether a close matters and how long the observation remains valid. A false breakout returns inside the prior structure instead of sustaining progress.

  • Context: preceding trend, volatility, nearby levels and scheduled events.
  • Evidence: closing location and volume relative to comparable periods.
  • Invalidation: a pre-written condition showing the idea no longer fits.
  • Alternative: the market can trend, range or reverse; consider more than one scenario.
04 / Technical analysis

Liquidity concepts without storytelling

Liquidity is the ability to transact size with limited price impact. Equal highs, equal lows and crowded stop locations are sometimes discussed as liquidity references. A quick move through a level is observable; claims about a particular institution intentionally hunting stops usually are not provable from candles alone.

  • A market-depth display is a snapshot and can change or cancel rapidly.
  • Order flow adds information, but does not eliminate uncertainty.
  • A setup is only a research hypothesis until costs, failures and out-of-sample behavior are examined.

PAUSE / APPLY / REFLECT

Make it your own.

Label ten swings using one fixed rule. Mark a range, a breakout, a successful retest and a failed breakout. Write the rule before looking at the later candles.

learn/indicators-and-volume.html:
TRADE ZUKO / Technical analysis

Indicators, volume and confirmation

Moving averages, RSI, VWAP, MACD, ATR and the limits of derived signals.

BY AMAN SINGH SUNEOLEARN · OBSERVE · REVIEW
ORIGINAL LEARNING GRAPHIC / NOT MARKET DATA
IN THIS CHAPTER01 · Indicators transform data; they do not create certainty02 · Momentum and volatility answer different questions03 · VWAP and volume need the right reference04 · Build a small, testable toolkitPractice & learning check

Original educational notes
Reviewed 21 September 2026

01 / Technical analysis

Indicators transform data; they do not create certainty

A simple moving average is an average over a lookback. An exponential moving average weights recent observations more heavily. Both lag the price data used to calculate them. Short lookbacks react faster and may be noisier; long lookbacks are smoother but slower.

  • Trend filters need explicit settings, data source and timeframe.
  • A crossover can whipsaw in a range.
  • Combining several price-derived indicators does not necessarily create independent confirmation.
WORKED EXAMPLE / FICTIONAL

Closes of 98, 100, 102, 104 and 106 have a five-period simple average of 102. The average describes those five closes, not the next one.

02 / Technical analysis

Momentum and volatility answer different questions

RSI compares recent gains and losses through a bounded momentum calculation. High RSI is not automatically a sell signal; strong trends can remain strong. MACD compares exponential averages and a signal line. ATR summarizes true ranges, including gaps; it measures movement, not direction.

  • RSI: momentum context, not a universal reversal timer.
  • MACD: trend/momentum changes with lag and whipsaw risk.
  • ATR: compare the scale of movement; a high value does not say up or down.
  • Bollinger Bands: dispersion around an average, not guaranteed reversal barriers.
03 / Technical analysis

VWAP and volume need the right reference

VWAP is a volume-weighted average of traded prices over a chosen session or anchor. A price above VWAP is a relationship to that reference, not an automatic reason to buy. Volume counts traded activity; derivatives open interest counts outstanding contracts. The measures are not interchangeable.

  • Compare volume with similar times of day; opening activity naturally differs from midday.
  • A spot index is a calculation, not a single traded instrument with its own cash share volume. Know which volume series your chart uses.
  • Some currency feeds show tick activity rather than complete global traded volume.
04 / Technical analysis

Build a small, testable toolkit

Write down the job of each tool: context, volatility, participation or trigger. Avoid adding another indicator whenever a losing example appears. Change one research variable at a time and retain an untouched evaluation sample.

  • State the condition in plain language before coding it.
  • Include flat periods, gaps and event sessions in the review.
  • Check whether a signal repaints, uses future information or depends on an unfinished bar.

PAUSE / APPLY / REFLECT

Make it your own.

Calculate a five-period SMA manually, then compare it with a shorter average. Explain why an RSI reading of 75 cannot alone prove a reversal.

learn/orders-and-execution.title: Orders, spreads and execution risk
learn/orders-and-execution.html:
TRADE ZUKO / Foundations

Orders, spreads and execution risk

Why a correct idea can still produce a different fill or a larger loss.

BY AMAN SINGH SUNEOLEARN · OBSERVE · REVIEW
ORIGINAL LEARNING GRAPHIC / NOT MARKET DATA
IN THIS CHAPTER01 · Market and limit orders make different trade-offs02 · A stop is a trigger, not insurance03 · Friction belongs in every example04 · Make the platform part of the learning planPractice & learning check

Original educational notes
Reviewed 21 September 2026

01 / Foundations

Market and limit orders make different trade-offs

A market order prioritizes execution at available prices; its fill price is not guaranteed. A limit order restricts the worst acceptable price but may remain unfilled or fill only partly. Availability and exact handling depend on the venue, instrument and broker.

  • A buy limit cannot execute above its limit under normal order rules, but it might not execute at all.
  • Displayed quantity can disappear before your order reaches the venue.
  • A large market order may consume several price levels.
02 / Foundations

A stop is a trigger, not insurance

A stop order activates according to its trigger conditions. A stop-market can fill far from the trigger during a gap or thin liquidity. A stop-limit adds a price boundary but may fail to close the position. Order types and segment restrictions differ; confirm current broker and exchange rules.

  • A target is a planned exit level, often implemented using a limit order; it is not a guaranteed profit.
  • A stop placed in software may behave differently from an exchange-held order.
  • Know what happens after a disconnection, rejection, partial fill or exchange halt.
WORKED EXAMPLE / FICTIONAL

An example position bought at 100 has a stop trigger at 98. If the next available bid is 95 after a gap, a stop-market could execute near 95. The planned 2-unit risk was not a maximum-loss guarantee.

03 / Foundations

Friction belongs in every example

Net outcome differs from a chart’s entry-to-exit move. Brokerage, exchange levies, taxes, the bid–ask spread, slippage and funding or borrowing charges may apply. Rules vary by instrument and can change. Use official schedules and a qualified tax professional for personal tax treatment.

  • Estimate costs before evaluating a strategy, then stress-test worse costs.
  • Do not count an unfilled limit order as a successful trade in a backtest.
  • Track rejection and partial-fill handling in a paper execution checklist.
04 / Foundations

Make the platform part of the learning plan

Use a watchlist, a clear layout and alerts whose trigger you understand. Learn position versus order views, quantity units, validity, leverage settings and the broker’s square-off policies. Two similar-looking tickets can have very different consequences.

  • Check symbol, exchange, expiry, quantity, order type and price before confirming any real order.
  • Paper trading is for learning mechanics; it may not reproduce queue position, emotional stress or true liquidity.
  • Never share credentials or give an unverified person remote control of an account.

PAUSE / APPLY / REFLECT

Using only a fictional order ticket, write how you would detect a wrong symbol, a wrong expiry and a ten-times-too-large quantity. Compare a stop-market gap with an unfilled stop-limit.

learn/risk-and-psychology.title: Risk, position size and the thinking trap
learn/risk-and-psychology.html:
TRADE ZUKO / Risk & process

Risk, position size and the thinking trap

Plan uncertain outcomes, understand drawdowns and build a review routine.

BY AMAN SINGH SUNEOLEARN · OBSERVE · REVIEW
ORIGINAL LEARNING GRAPHIC / NOT MARKET DATA
IN THIS CHAPTER01 · Translate an idea into a risk budget02 · Reward-to-risk is not a probability03 · Correlations and leverage change the picture04 · Use a process that survives emotionPractice & learning check

Original educational notes
Reviewed 21 September 2026

01 / Risk & process

Translate an idea into a risk budget

A research plan specifies the instrument, entry assumption, invalidation, exit process and quantity. Position size connects a price move to a cash outcome. A small-looking percentage change can create a large loss when quantity or leverage is large. There is no universally safe risk percentage.

  • For a simple long cash-share example: planned risk per share = entry minus stop, plus an allowance for costs and slippage.
  • A model quantity is the whole-number risk budget divided by planned risk per share, subject to available cash.
  • Actual gaps, liquidity and execution can produce a larger loss than the planned amount.
WORKED EXAMPLE / FICTIONAL

Fictional capital 100,000 and a study risk budget of 1,000 with 2.50 units of planned risk per share produce 400 shares before cash constraints. This is arithmetic, not a recommended allocation.

02 / Risk & process

Reward-to-risk is not a probability

A 2:1 planned reward-to-risk ratio describes the distances to two assumed exits. It says nothing by itself about the frequency of reaching each. Expectancy combines the probability and size of wins and losses, less costs. An attractive average can conceal rare large losses.

  • Expectancy = win probability × average win − loss probability × average loss − average costs.
  • A 40% win rate with average win 200 and average loss 100 has gross expectancy 20 per trade; costs of 25 make it negative.
  • A 20% drawdown requires a 25% gain on the remaining capital to recover. Loss and recovery percentages use different bases.
03 / Risk & process

Correlations and leverage change the picture

Several positions can express the same risk factor. Three bank stocks and a banking-index position may be more concentrated than four independent bets. Futures margin is collateral, not the maximum loss. Options spreads can have execution and settlement complications beyond a neat payoff diagram.

  • Stress-test a gap, a spread widening and a platform outage together.
  • Avoid funding a speculative plan with money needed for essential expenses or borrowing you cannot afford.
  • Daily stop rules and position limits are process controls, not loss guarantees.
04 / Risk & process

Use a process that survives emotion

FOMO, revenge trading, anchoring and confirmation bias distort decisions. A trading journal should compare your written process with what happened, not merely celebrate profitable outcomes. A rule-breaking win is not evidence that the rule-breaking was sound.

  • Before: event calendar, relevant levels, written scenarios and no-trade conditions.
  • During: follow the plan, record changes and pause when judgment is impaired.
  • After: save both successes and failures, including avoided trades and execution mistakes.
  • Review a sample over time; one result does not identify skill.

PAUSE / APPLY / REFLECT

Make it your own.

Use the practice lab to compare planned risk with a gap that doubles the stop distance. Explain why four correlated positions may not diversify risk.

learn/options-foundations.title: Options: rights, obligations and expiry
learn/options-foundations.html:
TRADE ZUKO / Options

Options: rights, obligations and expiry

Calls, puts, premium, intrinsic value, time value and contract risk.

BY AMAN SINGH SUNEOLEARN · OBSERVE · REVIEW
ORIGINAL LEARNING GRAPHIC / NOT MARKET DATA
IN THIS CHAPTER01 · Understand the contract before the chart02 · Intrinsic value is not profit03 · Time value, implied volatility and breakeven04 · Indian index and stock contracts need separate checksPractice & learning check

Original educational notes
Reviewed 21 September 2026

01 / Options

Understand the contract before the chart

A call gives its buyer a right under the contract to buy the underlying or receive the appropriate cash settlement. A put provides the corresponding selling right. The seller takes the obligation. Exercise style, expiry, underlying, multiplier and settlement method are part of the contract, not details to ignore.

  • A call buyer can benefit from upward movement, but time and volatility also affect the premium.
  • A put buyer can benefit from downward movement, subject to the same additional factors.
  • Bought options can expire worthless. Sellers face obligations, margin requirements and potentially very large losses.
02 / Options

Intrinsic value is not profit

At expiry, call intrinsic value per unit is max(underlying − strike, 0). Put intrinsic value is max(strike − underlying, 0). A simple long option’s expiry profit subtracts the premium paid and costs. Before expiry, pricing depends on more than intrinsic value.

  • In the money: positive intrinsic value.
  • At the money: underlying near the strike; the exact classification convention may vary.
  • Out of the money: no intrinsic value, yet the option can still have a premium before expiry.
WORKED EXAMPLE / FICTIONAL

A hypothetical call with strike 1,000 bought for 30 has intrinsic value 20 when expiry settlement is 1,020. The expiry outcome is a 10-unit loss before costs, despite being in the money.

03 / Options

Time value, implied volatility and breakeven

The premium above intrinsic value is often called time or extrinsic value. Time remaining, expected variability, rates and other contract factors influence pricing. A rise in the underlying does not guarantee a call buyer’s profit if other factors move unfavorably.

  • Simple long-call expiry breakeven: strike + premium, before costs.
  • Simple long-put expiry breakeven: strike − premium, before costs.
  • Expiry breakeven is not a universal price at which a pre-expiry position becomes profitable.
  • Implied volatility is an input inferred from option prices through a model; it is not a direction forecast.
04 / Options

Indian index and stock contracts need separate checks

Do not assume that an index option and an individual-stock option settle the same way. Check the current NSE contract specifications and your broker’s margin and settlement policies. Lot size, expiry schedules and eligible contracts can change.

  • Know the quantity multiplier before converting points into rupees.
  • Delivery obligations, exercise treatment and broker cutoffs can change practical risk.
  • Uncovered calls have theoretically unlimited loss; uncovered puts can have substantial downside. A seller’s margin is not a loss cap.

learn/option-chain-and-greeks.title: Nifty option chains and the Greeks
learn/option-chain-and-greeks.html:
TRADE ZUKO / Options

Nifty option chains and the Greeks

Read a chain as contract information, not a prediction machine.

BY AMAN SINGH SUNEOLEARN · OBSERVE · REVIEW
ORIGINAL LEARNING GRAPHIC / NOT MARKET DATA
IN THIS CHAPTER01 · Start with the same underlying and expiry02 · Open interest needs both sides of a contract03 · Four useful sensitivities04 · Volatility surfaces and eventsPractice & learning check

Original educational notes
Reviewed 21 September 2026

01 / Options

Start with the same underlying and expiry

An option chain groups calls and puts by strike for a selected expiry. Read the underlying reference, timestamp, bid and ask, quantities, last-traded price and settlement conventions. Stale last trades can make an apparently cheap option impossible to buy at that price.

  • Strike identifies the exercise reference; it is not the premium.
  • The bid–ask spread and depth affect executable prices.
  • Compare like-for-like expiries; different maturities contain different time and event exposure.
  • Our Nifty-style lab uses invented numbers, not a live feed or exchange trading signal.
02 / Options

Open interest needs both sides of a contract

Open interest counts outstanding contracts; volume counts traded activity during an interval. Every open contract has a long and a short side. An increase in open interest does not, by itself, prove bullish or bearish intent.

  • Opening and closing transactions can affect open interest differently.
  • High open interest is not a guaranteed support or resistance wall.
  • PCR, max pain and changes in open interest are contextual statistics, not reliable standalone forecasts.
  • Check the source’s units: contracts, lots and underlying quantity are not interchangeable.
03 / Options

Four useful sensitivities

Delta estimates sensitivity to a small underlying-price change. Gamma describes how delta changes. Theta estimates time-passage sensitivity; vega estimates sensitivity to implied volatility. These values come from models and move as conditions change.

  • Delta is not a fixed exposure or a guaranteed probability.
  • Near-expiry gamma can make exposure change quickly.
  • Bought options generally lose time value as time passes, other factors equal.
  • An implied-volatility fall can offset a favorable underlying move.
04 / Options

Volatility surfaces and events

Different strikes can show different implied volatilities, called skew or smile. Different expiries form a term structure. An event can raise option premiums beforehand and reduce them afterwards even when the underlying moves. Low premium does not necessarily mean low risk or good value.

  • Assess liquidity and missing or extreme IV readings before interpreting them.

01 / Options

Start with legs and cash flows

A strategy name hides a set of contracts. Write every leg: buy or sell, call or put, strike, expiry, quantity and premium. Then sum each leg’s result at the same assumed settlement price. The expiry picture does not describe every pre-expiry mark-to-market path.

  • Debit: premium paid to establish the structure.
  • Credit: premium received; this is not immediately earned profit.
  • Equal quantities and same expiry are crucial assumptions in a simple vertical-spread diagram.
02 / Options

Directional vertical spreads

A bull call spread buys a lower-strike call and sells a higher-strike call. In a simplified same-expiry model its maximum loss is the net debit and maximum gain is strike width minus debit. A bear put spread uses a higher-strike long put and a lower-strike short put. Credit spreads express the complementary payoff through short and protective long legs.

  • A bull put spread combines a short higher-strike put and a long lower-strike put.
  • A bear call spread combines a short lower-strike call and a long higher-strike call.
  • The advertised risk limit assumes the complete structure stays in place and settlement assumptions hold. Legging in or out can expose different risk.
03 / Options

Movement and range structures

A long straddle buys a call and a put at the same strike; enough movement is needed to overcome the combined premium at expiry. A long strangle uses separate out-of-the-money strikes. An iron condor combines a put credit spread below and a call credit spread above. It caps both favorable and unfavorable expiry outcomes in the simplified model.

  • A short straddle or strangle without protective wings can create very large or unlimited losses.
  • Butterflies concentrate a payoff around a region; small-looking debit does not imply a high chance of profit.
  • Calendar and diagonal spreads span expiries, so a single one-expiry intrinsic-value chart is insufficient.
  • Ratio spreads can leave excess uncovered options. Check the remaining tail exposure.
04 / Options

Hedging is a trade-off, not free protection

A protective put adds a purchased put to an underlying holding; insurance costs premium. A covered call caps upside while retaining substantial underlying downside. A collar combines a holding, a protective put and a short call, exchanging some upside for protection under stated terms.

  • Payoff labs here use hypothetical, European-style cash-settled, one-unit examples at expiry before costs.
  • Real outcomes depend on quantity, liquidity, exercise style, settlement, margin and broker handling.

01 / Stocks

A stock is a business claim

A share’s price reflects changing expectations about cash flows, growth, financing and risk. A good company is not automatically a good investment at every price. A price chart alone does not provide a full picture of debt, governance or dilution.

  • Read exchange filings and company results, not just summaries on social media.
  • Distinguish revenue, profit and operating cash flow.
  • Valuation ratios need comparable businesses and context; a low ratio can reflect genuine problems.
02 / Stocks

Context can move a group together

Sector demand, regulation, input costs and interest rates can affect related companies. Index weights mean large constituents can influence an index more than small constituents. Breadth asks how widely a move is shared.

  • Relative strength compares one series with another; it is not the same calculation as RSI.
  • A stock outperforming an index can still be falling in absolute terms.
  • Correlation changes through time, especially during stress.
03 / Stocks

Overnight holding creates event exposure

Swing and positional approaches face earnings surprises, corporate actions, announcements and global events while the domestic market is closed. The next opening price may jump past planned exits. A tight plotted stop does not eliminate gap risk.

  • Understand dividends, splits, rights issues and adjusted chart data.
  • Check scheduled company events before interpreting historical gaps.
  • Liquidity can deteriorate when everyone wants to exit together.
04 / Stocks

Build a research watchlist

Write the reason each symbol is included, the source date and the evidence that would contradict the idea. Separate business research from a technical timing experiment. Use paper observation first and review rejected ideas as well as attractive charts.

  • Record market context, company event, chart condition and invalidation.
  • Avoid survivorship bias: today’s successful companies are not the entire historical opportunity set.
  • Keep your research process separate from rumors or personalized recommendations.

01 / Crypto

Asset and venue are separate risks

Bitcoin and Ether are examples of crypto assets with different network designs and uses. Owning an asset through a venue adds platform and custody risk beyond the asset’s price. Crypto trading can run around the clock, but that does not mean liquidity or withdrawals are always available.

  • Spot ownership differs from a futures or perpetual contract.
  • A venue’s displayed balance is not proof that reserves, withdrawal access or legal protections are adequate.
  • Stablecoin is a category label, not a guarantee of a stable redemption value.
02 / Crypto

Custody determines who controls access

A private key controls the ability to authorize transactions for an address. With custodial services, access depends on the provider and its controls. Self-custody moves responsibility for keys, backups and transaction accuracy to the holder; mistakes can be irreversible.

  • Never share a seed phrase or private key.
  • Check the network and address carefully; similarly named tokens can be unrelated.
  • Beware impersonation, phishing, fake support and promises of guaranteed yield.
03 / Crypto

Perpetuals, funding and liquidation

Perpetual contracts generally have no scheduled expiry and use mechanisms such as funding payments to relate their prices to a reference. Funding conventions, mark prices, margin modes and liquidation rules differ by platform. Leverage magnifies sensitivity to relatively small price changes.

  • Initial margin is collateral, not a guaranteed maximum loss.
  • A liquidation price can change as collateral, fees, funding and position size change.
  • Cross margin can expose collateral beyond a single position; isolated configurations also have specific rules and risks.
  • Exchange failure, interruptions and rapid gaps are not captured by a tidy chart backtest.
04 / Crypto

Check local rules before considering participation

Product availability online is not proof that offering, accessing or funding it is lawful or appropriate where you live. Tax, reporting, exchange-control and platform rules differ and change. This library does not recommend an exchange, token or leveraged product.

  • Use official local sources and qualified advice for your circumstances.
  • An education example is not an invitation to bypass restrictions.
  • Keep the first exercises hypothetical: structure, cash flows, custody failure and adverse scenarios.

01 / Currencies

Read the quotation first

A currency pair expresses one currency in units of another. In USD/INR, the quote describes rupees per US dollar. If the quote rises, a dollar buys more rupees: the rupee has weakened against the dollar in that quotation. Inverting the pair reverses the numerical direction.

  • The first currency is the base and the second is the quote.
  • Pip and tick conventions depend on the instrument and venue.
  • A cash conversion, an exchange-traded derivative and an offshore leveraged CFD are different products.
02 / Currencies

Currencies reflect relative conditions

Interest-rate expectations, inflation, trade flows, capital flows and risk sentiment can all influence exchange rates. These factors interact and can already be reflected in price. A higher local interest rate does not mechanically guarantee a stronger currency.

  • Expected policy changes can matter more than the announcement itself.
  • Commodity prices can affect importing and exporting economies differently.
  • Central-bank communication and intervention are sources of uncertainty, not predictable trading rules.
03 / Currencies

Indian residents must use permitted routes

RBI guidance states that residents may undertake forex transactions only with authorized persons for permitted purposes. Electronic forex transactions must follow applicable rules for authorized electronic trading platforms or recognized exchanges. The existence of a foreign website is not authorization to use it.

  • Check RBI authorization, the permitted purpose and your eligibility—not merely an advertisement or app-store listing.
  • Do not assume offshore forex or CFD funding is allowed.
  • Recognized-exchange products also have eligibility, documentation and contract requirements.
  • Consult current RBI and exchange guidance before any real transaction.
04 / Currencies

Study contracts without importing the wrong assumptions

Currency futures and options have their own quotation, quantity, expiry and settlement rules. A chart labeled EUR/USD elsewhere is not automatically the same product available through an Indian broker. Holidays and international sessions can alter liquidity.

  • Verify exact contract specifications and broker support.
  • Include spread, costs and rollover or funding where applicable.

01 / Global markets

Follow a transmission channel, not a headline

A global event can affect Indian markets through earnings expectations, financing costs, currency movements, commodity prices or investors’ willingness to take risk. Different sectors may respond differently. The same headline can produce a different response in a different economic setting.

  • Higher oil can pressure some importers and benefit some producers; other variables can offset the effect.
  • Currency changes affect import costs and foreign revenues differently across companies.
  • Changes in global risk appetite can alter capital flows, without dictating every stock’s next move.
02 / Global markets

Expectations matter as much as the number

Markets react to information relative to what was already expected and positioned for. A strong data release may support earnings expectations yet raise concerns about tighter monetary policy. The net response is conditional, not a reliable one-line rule.

  • Compare release, prior value, revisions and a clearly sourced expectation.
  • Distinguish policy rates from market bond yields; long-term yields include expectations and risk compensation.
  • Do not infer causation from two charts moving together once.
03 / Global markets

Use an event map

Economic releases, central-bank decisions, earnings and geopolitical developments can change volatility. A calendar helps identify uncertainty; it does not predict the result. Time zones and daylight-saving changes matter when comparing overseas sessions with India.

  • India: RBI communications, inflation, activity indicators, fiscal policy and corporate results.
  • Global: major central-bank decisions, inflation and labor-market releases, oil developments and geopolitical risk.
  • Read official releases where possible and timestamp your observation.
04 / Global markets

Write two or more scenarios

A useful pre-session note separates known facts, uncertain outcomes and what would change the interpretation. Combine global context with domestic breadth, sector behavior, liquidity and actual price response. Never treat a macro opinion as permission to ignore risk.

  • Scenario A: conditions continue; what observable evidence would fit?
  • Scenario B: conditions disappoint or reverse; what would invalidate the first view?
  • No-trade condition: uncertainty or execution risk makes a paper observation more appropriate.

01 / Global markets

Know the instrument

GIFT Nifty refers to Nifty-related derivatives traded at NSE International Exchange in GIFT City. The flagship Nifty futures contract is US-dollar-denominated. It is a futures market referencing the Nifty 50, not the cash Nifty index itself and not the same instrument as a domestic ETF.

  • NSE IX operates in the international financial-services environment under its applicable framework.
  • The SGX Nifty transition to GIFT Nifty took place in 2023; old screenshots may use the earlier name.
  • Check current NSE IX specifications, trading hours, holidays and access requirements rather than relying on a fixed timetable from an old post.
02 / Global markets

Why people look at it before India opens

Trading outside the domestic cash session can reflect overseas news and changing risk sentiment while the Indian cash market is closed. That makes it a useful observation for context. Different timestamps, expiry contracts and liquidity mean comparisons need care.

  • Identify the contract month, timestamp and quote source.
  • Compare like-for-like futures observations, not an overnight futures quote with an unrelated spot timestamp.
  • A thin or stale quote can be misleading.
03 / Global markets

Understand the basis

Futures and spot need not trade at identical levels. Financing, expected dividends, time to expiry, liquidity and other market conditions influence the difference. A positive futures–spot gap is not automatically a prediction of an equally large cash-market gap.

  • Basis means futures price minus spot reference at a comparable time.
  • Different expiry contracts can have different basis values.
  • An overnight change can be partly or fully reversed before the cash open.

Use GIFT Nifty alongside overnight US and Asian conditions, oil, currencies, scheduled domestic events and fresh company information. After the Indian market opens, observe the actual cash-market response rather than forcing it to match an earlier cue.

Backtesting, journals, scanners, coding concepts and why a beautiful equity curve can mislead.

Original educational notes
Reviewed 21 September 2026

01 / Risk & process

Define a rule a second person can reproduce

A research idea needs explicit inputs, conditions, timing and exits. “Buy a strong breakout” is ambiguous. A testable version specifies the lookback, boundary, confirmation, signal time and fill assumption. That precision still does not establish a profitable edge.

  • Record the universe and dates before evaluating results.
  • Specify transaction costs, spread, slippage and whether shorting or leverage is permitted.
  • Avoid changing the rule every time a losing example appears.
02 / Risk & process

Separate development from evaluation

Use one sample for developing an idea and another untouched sample for evaluation. Walk-forward research repeats the process through successive periods. Trying many settings and reporting only the best is a form of selection bias.

  • Look-ahead bias uses information not available at the decision time.
  • Survivorship bias leaves out failed or delisted securities.
  • Overfitting captures historical noise instead of a repeatable relationship.
  • Include multiple market conditions and report uncertainty; a small sample can look excellent by chance.
03 / Risk & process

Learn what a backtester actually simulates

Pine Script strategies in TradingView model hypothetical orders and fills. Default assumptions, intrabar movement, gaps and transformed chart prices can change the result. An alert is not necessarily a completed order, and an automated connection introduces operational risk.

  • Begin with standard OHLC charts and inspect the simulator’s assumptions.
  • Check repainting and unfinished-bar behavior before comparing alerts with history.
  • Start coding with variables, conditions and plots; then add one explicit rule and realistic friction.
  • A screener finds candidates matching conditions; it does not verify their suitability or guarantee outcomes.
04 / Risk & process

Report more than the total return

Win rate, average win, average loss, costs, drawdown, trade count, concentration and time under water describe different parts of a result. Profit factor divides gross winning amounts by gross losing amounts; no losses in a tiny sample does not establish an infinite-quality strategy.

  • Review outliers and the sequence of outcomes, not only the average.
  • Compare paper assumptions with observed execution constraints.
  • Keep a versioned plan and journal; write what would make you stop researching an idea.
  • No historical test proves future profitability.

Build a written learning & trading plan

Bring context, rules, execution and review together without confusing a plan with a profit promise.

BY AMAN SINGH SUNEOLEARN · OBSERVE · REVIEW

IN THIS CHAPTER01 · Separate a learning goal from a money goal02 · Write a one-page decision framework03 · Run a paper exercise from start to finish04 · End with a review, not a verdict on yourselfPractice & learning check

Original educational notes
Reviewed 21 September 2026

01 / Risk & process

Separate a learning goal from a money goal

A learning goal is observable: explain a contract, calculate a payoff or identify an invalidation rule. A daily income target does not make the market offer a suitable opportunity. Begin with what you need to understand and how you will check that understanding.

  • Choose one instrument family and one observation timeframe for a study exercise.
  • List the missing knowledge before attempting a strategy: contract, liquidity, costs and settlement.
  • Keep essential spending and personal financial commitments outside a speculative experiment.
02 / Risk & process

Write a one-page decision framework

A repeatable framework records the market context, the condition being studied, the assumptions behind it and the evidence that would contradict it. Include a no-trade condition. A plan is useful because it exposes decisions to review, not because it makes outcomes certain.

  • Context: date, data source, event calendar, trend or range and nearby reference zones.
  • Hypothesis: precise condition, observation time and alternative explanation.
  • Risk: fictional entry, invalidation, quantity calculation, friction and adverse-gap scenario.
  • Execution: order assumptions, partial fills, rejects and what happens if the platform disconnects.
03 / Risk & process

Run a paper exercise from start to finish

Record the plan before revealing the next prices. Document whether the assumed entry could plausibly fill, including spread and available information at that time. If a rule changes during the exercise, preserve the original version and explain the change rather than rewriting history.

  • Collect both fitting and non-fitting examples, not only winners.
  • Separate process adherence from the financial result.
  • Use a fixed evaluation sample and do not turn a few paper wins into a claim of live readiness.
WORKED EXAMPLE / FICTIONAL

A fictional plan may say: observe whether a defined range is broken on a completed bar; do nothing during a scheduled release; record a failed break as well as a continuing move. This is a study protocol, not a recommended entry rule.

04 / Risk & process

End with a review, not a verdict on yourself

Review decisions, data quality, execution assumptions and uncertainty. A losing example can teach something useful; a profitable example can still rely on a bad assumption. Decide what to study next and what evidence would make you abandon the idea.

  • Use the local journal to record observation, evidence, alternative scenario and review.
  • Check your understanding with the lesson questions and work through losing payoff examples.
  • Read current official rules before any real transaction; seek qualified help for personal financial decisions.
  • The goal of this library is understanding. It does not certify competence or establish that trading is suitable for you.

Reversal01

Double top

Two nearby highs with an intervening low after an advance. The low is often called the neckline.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Define the two-high tolerance, intervening swing and a break rule before testing.

How it can fail

A second high alone is incomplete. Price can break above both highs or reclaim the neckline.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Reversal02

Double bottom

Two nearby lows separated by a rebound after a decline.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Locate the intervening high and compare the lows within a zone, not an exact tick.

How it can fail

A second low can be followed by a fresh low; an apparent neckline break can reverse.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Reversal03

Triple top

Three tests of a similar upper area with pullbacks between them.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Observe spacing, prior trend and the shared lower boundary.

How it can fail

Repeated tests can end in an upside breakout instead of reversal.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Reversal04

Triple bottom

Three tests of a similar lower area with rebounds between them.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Study the upper boundary and whether price actually leaves the range.

How it can fail

Support can fail. Counting three lows does not establish future demand.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Reversal05

Head & shoulders

Three peaks: a higher middle peak between two lower shoulders.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Mark a neckline connecting the pullback lows; it can slope. Study closes and failed breaks.

How it can fail

The right shoulder is uncertain until later price develops; an upside recovery invalidates a bearish reading.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Reversal06

Inverse head & shoulders

Three troughs: a deeper middle trough between two shallower shoulders.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Mark the rebound highs forming the neckline and define completion in advance.

How it can fail

A breakout can fail, or price can return to the head region.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Reversal07

Rounding bottom

A gradual transition from falling prices through a base into rising prices.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Use enough surrounding history to distinguish a base from a short bounce.

How it can fail

The curve can flatten or resume the downtrend; smooth textbook arcs are rare.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Reversal08

Rounding top

A gradual loss of upward momentum followed by a rolling decline.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Check the broader trend and avoid drawing a curve merely because you know the outcome.

How it can fail

A pause can resolve upward and negate the rounded-top interpretation.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Continuation / two-way09

Ascending triangle

Rising swing lows meet a roughly horizontal upper boundary.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Watch both boundaries. A break can occur in either direction despite the common bullish interpretation.

How it can fail

Price can fall through the rising lower boundary or briefly break resistance and return.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Continuation / two-way10

Descending triangle

Falling swing highs meet a roughly horizontal lower boundary.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Define a boundary-break rule and distinguish an incomplete contraction from a completed break.

How it can fail

Price can break upward or reclaim the lower boundary after a false breakdown.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Continuation / two-way11

Symmetrical triangle

Lower highs and higher lows form converging boundaries.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

The contraction describes compression; it does not determine the eventual direction.

How it can fail

Breakouts can fail and late apex noise can be hard to interpret.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Reversal12

Rising wedge

Both boundaries rise while the swings contract. Often studied for weakening upward progress.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Draw both rising boundaries with multiple touches and assess the preceding trend.

How it can fail

It can continue upward. A shape alone is not a confirmed downside reversal.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Reversal13

Falling wedge

Both boundaries fall while the swings contract. Often studied for slowing downward progress.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Look for multiple touches and a clearly specified break condition.

How it can fail

It can continue lower; the same outline in a different context can behave differently.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Continuation / two-way14

Bull flag

A sharp rise followed by a smaller, often downward-sloping consolidation.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Compare the correction with the prior move and inspect participation and nearby resistance.

How it can fail

The correction can become a reversal; a breakout can immediately re-enter the flag.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Continuation / two-way15

Bear flag

A sharp fall followed by a smaller, often upward-sloping consolidation.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Define the flag boundaries and evaluate whether downward progress actually resumes.

How it can fail

The consolidation can develop into a durable recovery.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Continuation / two-way16

Bull pennant

A strong upward move followed by a compact converging pause.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Separate the impulse from the contraction and avoid assuming continuation before a break.

How it can fail

A downside break or stalled follow-through can invalidate the interpretation.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Continuation / two-way17

Bear pennant

A strong downward move followed by a compact converging pause.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Study both the short-term contraction and higher-timeframe context.

How it can fail

The pause may resolve upward instead of extending the decline.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Continuation / two-way18

Rectangle / range

Repeated swings between two approximately horizontal areas.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Mark zones, not perfect lines, and study the eventual break separately from range touches.

How it can fail

Either side can break; false breaks and repeated whipsaws are common study cases.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Continuation / two-way19

Cup & handle

A rounded recovery toward an old high followed by a smaller pullback.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Distinguish the cup from the handle and inspect whether the upper region is actually exceeded.

How it can fail

The handle can deepen or the recovery can fail; not every U-shape is a valid setup.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Continuation / two-way20

Broadening formation

Higher highs and lower lows create expanding swings.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Recognize increasing range and uncertainty rather than forcing a directional prediction.

How it can fail

Stops and sizing based on earlier quiet movement may underestimate later volatility.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick21

Doji

Open and close are close together relative to the interval’s range.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Compare the surrounding trend, location and subsequent action.

How it can fail

A doji is not automatic reversal; an ongoing trend can continue.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick22

Hammer

A small body near the top of the range with a long lower wick, often studied after a decline.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

The prior decline and nearby zone matter as much as the silhouette.

How it can fail

Price can break beneath the wick or fail to develop upward follow-through.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick23

Hanging man

Hammer-like geometry appearing after an advance. The context changes the name.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Study the preceding advance and later action; the candle alone does not establish reversal.

How it can fail

A long lower wick can be absorbed and the uptrend can resume.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick24

Shooting star

A small body near the bottom of the range with a long upper wick, commonly studied after an advance.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Locate the candle within the surrounding trend and resistance zones.

How it can fail

An upper wick can be followed by renewed buying and a higher high.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick25

Inverted hammer

Shooting-star-like geometry after a decline rather than an advance.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Do not confuse geometry with confirmation; record later price behavior separately.

How it can fail

The decline can continue beneath the candle’s low.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick26

Bullish engulfing

An upward real body encloses the preceding downward real body. Wick engulfment is a different, stricter condition.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Compare real bodies consistently and consider the preceding decline and zone.

How it can fail

Engulfing bodies inside congestion can have little significance; lows can still fail.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick27

Bearish engulfing

A downward real body encloses the preceding upward real body.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Specify whether your definition compares bodies or the whole range.

How it can fail

A large red candle can be reversed on the next interval.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick28

Inside bar

The second bar’s high and low lie inside the previous bar’s high and low.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

It describes contraction, with potential breaks in either direction.

How it can fail

A first break can reverse through the other side; direction is not determined by the name.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick29

Morning star

A downward candle, a small transitional body and a recovering upward candle form a three-candle sequence.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Classic gap requirements depend on market/session convention; make your definition explicit.

How it can fail

Recovery may be shallow or fail. Continuous markets often do not show textbook gaps.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick30

Evening star

An upward candle, a small transitional body and a falling candle form a three-candle sequence.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Assess the prior advance and the third candle’s penetration into the first body.

How it can fail

The apparent reversal can be followed by a new high.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick31

Tweezer bottom

Adjacent candles test a similar low area; their bodies can differ.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Use a tolerance suited to the instrument rather than demanding an identical tick.

How it can fail

Repeated lows can break; two touches do not prove lasting support.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

Candlestick32

Marubozu / full body

A large body with very short or absent wicks describes a strong net interval move.

Study the context & failure +

What to investigate

Compare size with recent ranges and distinguish an opening move from an exhausted move.

How it can fail

A strong completed candle does not prevent the next interval from reversing.

Practice: find one example that fits and one that fails. Fix your rules before revealing the later candles. Illustrations show geometry, not recommended entries or price targets.

THE MARKET LAB / START WITH UNDERSTANDING

Behind every candle,

Trading is the buying and selling of financial instruments. Price changes as orders meet; charts summarize those transactions. Understanding the mechanics comes before taking any risk.

LAB
01—04
01 / CONTEXT

Trading isn’t investing.

Trading usually focuses on shorter-term price changes. Investing generally has a longer horizon and looks at the underlying business or asset. Neither approach removes the possibility of loss.

02 / OBSERVATION

Price action tells a story.

Read the open, high, low and close alongside swing highs, swing lows, zones and volume. A pattern is an observation to test in context—not a promise about the next candle.

03 / SURVIVAL

Risk comes first.

Leverage magnifies losses as well as gains. Learn position sizing, transaction costs, slippage and why a stop order cannot guarantee an exit price. Paper practice is not proof of real-world profitability.

02 / PRICE ACTION, MADE VISIBLE

Learn to read
one candle first.

THE READING ORDER

A small shape.
Four useful clues.

  1. 01
    The body

    The distance between open and close. A larger body means a larger net move over that interval, not necessarily a better trading opportunity.

  2. 02
    The wicks

    The extremes reached above and below the body. A wick alone does not who traded, why they traded or where price will go.

  3. 03
    The surrounding chart

    Compare the candle with nearby price swings, the timeframe and volume. The same shape can occur in very different market conditions.

Strike & expiry: identify the contract.

The strike is the contract’s reference price. Expiry is when it ends. Compare calls and puts for the same expiry. At a 24,000 index level, the 24,000 strike is at the money; lower strikes have positive call intrinsic value, and higher strikes have positive put intrinsic value.

BEYOND DIRECTION / FOUR RISK SENSITIVITIES

An index can move your way.
Your option can still lose value.

Greeks estimate sensitivity with other factors held constant. They change with market conditions; they are not fixed promises.

Δ

Delta / direction

How much the premium is estimated to change for a small move in the underlying.

Γ

Gamma / acceleration

How delta changes as the underlying moves. Sensitivity can change quickly near expiry.

Θ

Theta / passing time

The effect of time passing. Bought options generally lose time value, all else equal.

ν

Vega / volatility

Sensitivity to implied volatility. Falling IV can reduce a bought option’s premium.

!

Know the downside before studying the upside.

An option buyer can lose the entire premium paid, plus costs. Uncovered option selling can involve much larger losses; an uncovered call’s loss is theoretically unlimited. Intrinsic value is not profit. These examples exclude lot size, transaction costs and settlement details.

Contract specifications, expiry rules and lot sizes can change. Check the exchange and your broker before making any real-world decision. This page does not recommend a strike, expiry or strategy.
